analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to enroll workers and families in private or a new public health insurance plan, aiming for universal coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate vote: it sat in the Finance Committee after one day of hearings until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every employer to enroll full-time employees and their families in an approved private health plan or in a new government-run public health insurance plan, administered like Medicare. Everyone not otherwise covered could enroll in the public plan, with premiums tied to income, low-income assistance, no denial for pre-existing conditions, and a yearly cap on out-of-pocket costs of $3,000. It also set federal standards for private plans, guaranteed issue and renewal for small-employer plans, expanded community health centers, and funded it through premiums on employers and individuals plus a progressive financing requirement. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, got one day of hearings, and never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The uninsured and underinsured gain guaranteed access to a basic health benefit package; workers gain protection against pre-existing condition exclusions and cost-sharing caps; low-income enrollees get premium assistance; self-employed people gain a full tax deduction for health insurance; small employers get a refundable credit and guaranteed-issue rules; community health centers get expanded funding.

how_it_helps.text: Every employer must enroll full-time employees and their family members in a qualified employer health plan or a new public plan, closing the largest gap in coverage.

U.S. residents who are not otherwise covered are eligible to enroll in a public health insurance plan covering basic services including hospital care, physician services, and preventive care, with a $3,000 annual cap on deductibles and coinsurance.

Low-income individuals get assistance limiting or eliminating premiums and cost-sharing, and children get full EPSDT screening, dental, vision, and hearing services regardless of employment-based enrollment.
Private plans cannot deny or limit basic coverage based on health status, and small-employer plans must guarantee issue and renewal and use community rating.
Self-employed individuals get a full, permanent deduction for health insurance costs, and very small businesses get a refundable credit for plan costs.
Funding must be progressive in the aggregate, sufficient to cover the plan's net costs, and not drawn from any single age group.

analysis.who_pays: Employers owe premiums tied to payroll (or must buy coverage) for full-time, most part-time, and seasonal workers; individuals owe premiums for public-plan enrollment, with an individual coverage requirement enforced through tax returns and doubled back-premiums for non-enrollment; providers face Medicare-style payment rates under the public plan; the federal government covers its share through appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Employers can pass up to 20% of the plan's actuarial cost to employees as premiums, and workers face deductibles and coinsurance up to the $3,000 cap, so coverage is not free.

After full phase-in, every eligible individual is required to be covered; the Treasury collects enrollment information with tax returns and can charge twice the normal premiums to people who did not enroll on time.

The public plan pays providers using Medicare payment rules with no administrative or judicial review of rates, which providers would bear as lower reimbursement, and it allows no review of the actuarial rates charged to enrollees either.
Mental health and substance abuse coverage is capped at 45 inpatient days and 25 outpatient visits per year, and prescription drugs were not included pending a cost-effectiveness study.

The employer mandate is phased in over four to six years with exceptions for small employers that meet coverage targets, collective bargaining agreements, and Puerto Rico and territories, so universal coverage would arrive slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a broad, enforceable guarantee of coverage for significant burdens on employers and an individual coverage requirement with tax-enforced penalties. Its public plan competes with private insurers using Medicare rates, which was its cost-control strength and its political weakness. Its phase-in schedule, mental health limits, and exclusion of prescription drugs make it a partial, not comprehensive, benefit package. On balance it would have guaranteed coverage to tens of millions at the cost of a new payroll-based financing system and an individual mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, got one day of hearings in June 1992, was never voted out of committee, and died when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Rockefeller introduced the bill on May 23, 1991 and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee held hearings on June 9, 1992, its only action beyond referral.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and was never reported out of committee or scheduled for a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed payroll-based premiums and insurers who would have faced a government-run competitor are better off; the bill's intended beneficiaries, the uninsured, gained nothing because it never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers; the uninsured gained nothing

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to implement the Pepper Commission's universal-coverage proposal and pursued hearings in the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, held one day of hearings on June 9, 1992, and never reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on and no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of any potential coalition is unknown; with zero cosponsors the bill never generated an observable floor coalition at all.

industries.note: Every employer would have had to pay premiums tied to wages or buy qualified coverage for nearly all workers, including most part-time and seasonal staff, with penalties up to three times owed premiums for violations. Small employers get credits and delayed phase-in, but the mandate is the bill's core cost.

Insurers would have gained a large enrollment base through the employer mandate and qualification standards that lock in a private-plan role, but they would have faced guaranteed-issue, community-rating, and pre-existing condition rules, plus competition from a Medicare-administered public plan paying Medicare rates.

industries.industry: Managed care organizations and utilization review firms
industries.note: The bill gives managed care favorable treatment and preempts state laws restricting managed care plans and utilization review that meet federal standards, expanding their role in the new coverage system.

industries.industry: Hospitals, physicians, and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers would have gained tens of millions of newly insured paying customers, but the public plan would have paid them under Medicare rules with rates adjusted downward for the new population and no judicial review, and malpractice studies pointed toward future cost containment.

industries.industry: Community health centers and public health clinics
industries.note: Authorizations for immunization, TB, lead poisoning, family planning, migrant and community health centers, and homeless and HIV services are extended, and the public plan's trust fund funds grants to expand primary care centers.
